planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, since germination is slow and erratic at cool temperatures; transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing.

directions: Monarch is a widely grown European celeriac that holds the Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its reliable, high-yielding globes. Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant out into deeply worked, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, setting plants at the same depth they grew in their cells. Keep the bed evenly moist all season and strip away side shoots and surface rootlets as the crown swells to encourage a smooth, round, white-fleshed globe. Harvest once roots reach 3-5 inches across; Monarch stores well through winter in a cool root cellar or can be left in the ground under mulch in milder climates.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant to the garden after danger of hard frost has passed and soil has warmed somewhat.

directions: Mars is an organically bred celeriac selection grown for its large, uniform, bulbous roots and clean celery flavor. Sow seed indoors in flats or cell trays, barely covering it, since light aids germination, and keep consistently moist and warm until seedlings emerge. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil and water deeply and regularly through the season, since any moisture stress produces hollow or cracked roots. Harvest in fall once the knobby crown reaches full size, trimming the fibrous lower rootlets before cooking or storing in damp sand.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; this fast-growing F1 can be transplanted out slightly earlier than open-pollinated types since it matures quickly once warm weather arrives.

directions: President is a vigorous European F1 hybrid celeriac prized by market growers for forming large, clean, smooth-skinned white roots faster than many open-pollinated types. Start seed indoors in cell trays and transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil once frost danger has passed, setting plants slightly deeper than they grew to help anchor the developing globe. Water consistently through summer and remove lower leaves and surface rootlets periodically to keep the crown clean. Roots size up reliably even in shorter growing seasons, making President a good choice where summers are cool or compressed.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing.

directions: Balena is a Bejo-bred F1 celeriac known for its relatively early maturity and large, round, smooth-skinned roots with few surface rootlets, making it a favorite for growers who want less trimming at harvest. Sow indoors and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil after frost danger passes, then keep the bed evenly watered all season, since fluctuating moisture leads to cracked or hollow globes. Strip off lower leaves and side shoots periodically to channel energy into the swelling root. Harvest once roots reach full size in fall; Balena stores well in cold, humid conditions for winter use.

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep as early as 2-4 weeks before last frost into deeply worked, stone-free soil; roots fork badly in compacted or rocky ground.

directions: Russian Giant is a high-yielding European scorzonera selection grown for its long, sweet, black-skinned roots with creamy white flesh. Sow thinly and directly in the garden, since scorzonera resents transplanting, and thin seedlings to 4-6 inches apart once established. Keep the deeply dug bed evenly moist through the long growing season to encourage straight, unforked roots. Roots can be harvested in the first autumn but develop their best flavor after overwintering in the ground and being dug the following spring; peel freshly dug roots under water, since the cut ends ooze a bitter milky latex.

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep as early as 2-4 weeks before last frost into deeply worked, loose soil free of stones so roots can grow long and straight.

directions: Enorma is a market-grower favorite scorzonera variety producing long, straight, black-skinned roots averaging 9-11 inches long with a rich, savory, mildly sweet flavor often compared to oysters or artichoke hearts. Direct sow thinly in deeply cultivated soil, since the long taproots need unobstructed depth to size up properly, and thin to final spacing once seedlings have their first true leaves. Water consistently through summer and fall. Harvest roots in autumn or leave them in the ground through winter for an even sweeter spring harvest; the tender young shoots and flower buds that emerge in spring are also edible.

common_name: Waldspindel Jerusalem Artichoke (Austrian Red Fingerling Sunchoke)

planting.note: Plant whole or cut seed tubers with at least one or two eyes 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil once soil can be worked in spring; choose a permanent bed, since any tuber left behind will resprout.

directions: Waldspindel (German for 'forest spindle') is an Austrian heirloom Jerusalem artichoke prized for its small, elongated, deep red-skinned fingerling tubers, which are easier to clean than the knobby tubers of unnamed sunchoke stock. Plant seed tubers in spring in loose, fertile soil in full sun; stems grow thick and lush, somewhat shorter and stockier than tall field types such as Fuseau. Tall late-summer sunflower-like blooms are followed by a fall tuber harvest that can continue through winter and into early spring wherever the ground is workable, with flavor and sweetness improving after exposure to cold.

planting.note: Direct sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest after frost sweetens the roots; thin seedlings to final spacing once established.

directions: Gowrie is a traditional Scottish rutabaga selection grown for its sweet, round, purple-topped roots with firm golden flesh, used historically as the base for Scottish 'neeps and tatties.' Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in the garden in mid to late summer, thinning seedlings to 6-8 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Roots mature in fall and develop their best flavor after exposure to light frost, which converts starches to sugars. Harvest and store in a cool root cellar, or leave roots in the ground under heavy mulch in milder climates for a winter-long harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow in mid to late summer so roots mature with cooling fall weather; thin to final spacing once seedlings are established.

directions: Angela is a refined English selection of the classic purple-top rutabaga, bred originally for the UK market and valued for its attractive purple-and-cream roots, light golden flesh, and winter hardiness. Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in mid to late summer, thinning to a final spacing of 6-8 inches. Keep the bed consistently moist to avoid woody or cracked roots. Harvest after a light frost sweetens the flesh, and store roots in a cool, humid root cellar or leave them in the ground under mulch through winter in milder climates.

planting.note: Direct sow in summer, allowing a longer season than most rutabagas, so roots size up before fall harvest; thin seedlings to final spacing.

directions: Joan produces uniform, round roots with purple tops and pale flesh that is sweet and mild even when harvested young, though it also sizes up well for longer fall storage. Direct sow in fertile, well-worked soil and thin to a final spacing of 6-8 inches, watering consistently through the growing season to prevent woody texture. Because Joan takes somewhat longer to mature than many rutabagas, sow it earlier in summer than quicker varieties to ensure roots finish sizing before hard freezes. Harvest after light frost for the best flavor and store in a cool, humid cellar through winter.

common_name: Marian Rutabaga (Large Yellow Purple Top Swede)

planting.note: Direct sow in summer for a fall harvest; this relatively quick-maturing rutabaga can be sown a bit later than slower varieties.

directions: Marian produces large, yellow-fleshed roots with purple tops that can size up to 8 inches across while remaining sweet and fine-grained. Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in summer and thin to a final spacing of 6-8 inches, keeping the bed evenly watered to avoid pithy or cracked roots. Marian matures somewhat faster than many storage rutabagas, making it useful where the fall growing window is shorter. Harvest after a light frost and store in a cool root cellar, where roots keep their flavor and texture for several months.

common_name: Sunset Oca (Early High-Yielding Andean Wood Sorrel)

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost; Sunset begins tuberizing roughly two weeks earlier than most oca varieties, which helps it finish bulking in shorter-summer climates.

directions: Sunset is among the highest-yielding oca varieties available in North America, reported to produce over two pounds of tubers per plant under good conditions. Plant seed tubers in loose, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Sunset is a vigorous early sprouter with green stems and foliage, and it initiates tuber formation about two weeks earlier than most other oca strains once day length shortens in late summer. Tubers emerge yellowish-orange with red eyes and develop a carrot-like, slightly sweet flavor after a period of post-harvest sun exposure. Harvest after the first frost kills back the foliage.

common_name: Royal Roja Oca (Magenta Andean Wood Sorrel)

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost in loose, well-drained soil; like other oca, tuber formation is triggered by shortening autumn day length.

directions: Royal Roja is a productive oca variety named for its striking bright magenta tuber skin, which holds its color well after cooking. Plant tubers in full sun to partial shade in loose, well-drained soil of nearly any pH, and grow exactly as other oca: the sprawling, clover-like foliage needs a long frost-free season to bulk up tubers, which form only after days shorten in autumn. Harvest after the first frost kills the foliage, typically in the November-to-January window. As with other oca, let freshly dug tubers sit in a sunny spot for several days to convert starch to sugar and mellow the tartness before eating.

common_name: Winter Sun Oca (Orange Pink-Eyed Andean Wood Sorrel)

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost in loose, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Winter Sun produces plump, brilliant orange tubers with contrasting pink eyes, among the more visually striking oca varieties grown in North America. Plant tubers in loose, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the sprawling, succulent-stemmed foliage grows through summer and only begins forming tubers once autumn days shorten. Harvest after frost kills back the top growth, typically from November into January depending on climate. Spread freshly dug tubers in a sunny spot outdoors for several days after harvest, which both deepens their orange color and sweetens the otherwise tart, oxalic-acid-rich flesh.

common_name: Mexican Red Oca (Dark Red Andean Wood Sorrel)

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost; tuber initiation occurs after the fall equinox as days shorten, with harvest following the first killing frost.

directions: Mexican Red is an oca strain grown in the mountains of Mexico, distinguished by its dark, blood-red, flattened-cylindrical tubers with a crisp, apple-like texture and a flavor ranging from mildly sweet to tangy. Plant tubers in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; the tall, sprawling plants produce tubers on intermediate-to-long stolons, so give them room to spread or mound soil around the base as they grow. Tuber initiation begins after the fall equinox and continues until frost kills the foliage, which signals it's time to dig. The reddish color holds up reasonably well in cooking, turning a muted red when boiled or roasted.

planting.note: Set out rhizome crown divisions around last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give this tall-growing strain extra staking or wind shelter since it often exceeds 7 feet by season's end.

directions: New Zealand is a widely grown heirloom yacon strain, likely originally from Ecuador but long cultivated commercially in New Zealand, valued for reliable production across a range of climates. Propagate from the knobby rhizome crowns saved from the base of the previous year's stalks, not from the large storage roots, which have no buds and will not sprout. Set divisions out after the last frost in deep, fertile soil, since this is one of the tallest yacon strains and continues growing even after flowering begins. The tan tubers develop purple-red blushing with exposure and have the species' typical sweet, crisp, watery texture, best after a week or two of post-harvest curing in a warm, sunny spot.

common_name: Blanco Yacon (Early White Andean Ground Apple)

planting.note: Set out rhizome crown divisions around last frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Blanco flowers at an intermediate date and finishes somewhat earlier than later-flowering yacon strains.

directions: Blanco, previously sold as 'Early White,' is one of the two most common yacon strains grown in North America and has been in cultivation here since the mid-1990s. Propagate from rhizome crown divisions rather than storage roots, and set out after last frost in deep, fertile soil in full sun; plants reach a medium height of about six feet with reddish stems. Tubers are tan-skinned, developing light red blushing with extended light exposure, and the white flesh is moderately sweet with the characteristic crisp, juicy texture of yacon. Dormant rhizomes store for two to three months under cool, dry conditions if the growing season ends before replanting.
